description:
Programme or Project Overview

The University of Copenhagen offers a Marie Sklodowska-Curie Actions (MSCA) doctoral candidate position in the E-CoRe doctoral network, working on reversible programming languages as doctoral candidate DC1. Reversible computing studies programming models and languages in which computation can run backwards as well as forwards, with applications from energy-efficient computing to quantum programming and incremental computation.

The E-CoRe network trains doctoral candidates across European partner institutions with a structured programme of secondments, network-wide schools and joint supervision. The DC1 project at the University of Copenhagen's Department of Computer Science (DIKU) develops semantic and logical foundations for reversible languages, building on the department's leading role in this research area.

MSCA conditions and eligibility

As an MSCA doctoral candidate, the researcher receives a generous doctoral allowance plus mobility allowance under the MSCA unit rates, implemented through the Danish employment system. MSCA mobility rules apply: candidates must not have resided or carried out their main activity in Denmark for more than 36 months in the 36 months immediately before the call deadline. Applicants hold a master's degree (or equivalent) in computer science or a related field, and the working language of the network is English.

Highlights

  • Reversible programming languages and semantics
  • Logical foundations of invertible computation
  • Quantum and energy-efficient computing connections
  • MSCA network training, secondments and schools
  • Leading reversible-computing group at DIKU
  • MSCA doctoral allowance plus mobility allowance

About University of Copenhagen

The University of Copenhagen is Denmark's oldest and largest research university, founded in 1479. Its six faculties cover health and medical sciences, humanities, law, science, social sciences and theology, and the university consistently ranks among the leading research institutions in Europe. Doctoral training is organised through the university's graduate schools, where salaried PhD positions and externally funded doctoral networks, including Marie Sklodowska-Curie actions, are advertised on the employment portal. A large share of the academic community is international, and English is the working language in most research environments.
